section_summary: This section follows American and British oil companies’ negotiations over Japan’s Petroleum Industry Law, especially its requirement to store six months of oil. An April 1935 understanding promised relief, but opposition among Japanese ministries delayed a lasting settlement; by September, enforcement had been postponed to June 1936. The section also covers oil business in Korea and Manchuria, boycott rumors, and a possible American treaty objection to storage imposed for national defense.

subfiles.title: Report on oil negotiations and Manchukuoan kerosene duties, concluding pages
subfiles.about: Reports a pause in oil talks and joint American and British representations over discriminatory Manchukuoan customs duties.
subfiles.summary: The oil companies agreed to suspend talks until after the Diet session. American and British embassy officials asked Japan to help end duties favoring Japanese light oil over American and British kerosene.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1255: American Oil Interests in Japan
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports an April understanding that temporarily eased foreign oil companies’ concerns under Japan’s Petroleum Industry Law.
subfiles.summary: After talks nearly collapsed, representations by oil executives, the British Ambassador and W. Cameron Forbes preceded Japanese assurances on quotas, prices, nondiscrimination and a proposed reduction of storage obligations to three months. Grew says the understanding must remain quiet while regulations are changed. He notes the companies still face the October deadline unless Japan acts, and discusses a possible refusal to supply crude oil to Japan.

subfiles.title: Outline of understanding with Shokosho officials
subfiles.about: Records Japanese officials’ answers to five points raised by Standard-Vacuum and Rising Sun Petroleum.
subfiles.summary: The outline records affirmative answers on minimum 1935 gallonage, a fair share of future growth, three months’ storage including working stocks, cost-based prices and nondiscrimination. It lists participants and notes that no fixed-term guarantee was given.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of conversation with Kurusu
subfiles.about: Records Kurusu’s qualifications to the oil companies’ outline of the April understanding.
subfiles.summary: Kurusu generally confirmed the outline but reserved the Korean question and said changing storage rules required an Imperial Ordinance.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on proposed crude oil supply refusal
subfiles.about: Clarifies whether a reported Anglo-Dutch and California oil supply refusal concerned Japan or only Manchuria Oil Company.
subfiles.summary: Sir Robert Clive understood the proposal to concern Japan as a whole, but said recent talks had changed the situation.

subfiles.title: Reply to W. C. Teagle
subfiles.about: Acknowledges thanks for U.S. assistance in petroleum negotiations.
subfiles.summary: Hull welcomes Teagle’s appreciation and forwards the letter to the Tokyo Embassy.

subfiles.title: Letter forwarding Teagle’s appreciation
subfiles.from: William Phillips, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Forwards Teagle’s letter and commends the embassy’s work.
subfiles.summary: Phillips sends Grew Teagle’s appreciation and commends the embassy staff’s assistance in the oil negotiations.

subfiles.title: File note: Report of Boycott of Japan and Manchukuo
subfiles.about: Indexes a Dairen consular report on a rumored foreign oil boycott.
subfiles.summary: Cross-references the Dairen despatch concerning boycott reports.

subfiles.title: Report of Boycott of Japan and Manchukuo by Foreign Oil Firms
subfiles.from: Stuart E. Gromon, American Consul, Dairen
subfiles.about: Reports boycott rumors, changes in Dairen oil business and a Soviet trader’s view.
subfiles.summary: The consul relays press rumors of a British and American oil boycott but knows of no foreign company withdrawal from Dairen. He reports a transfer of Asiatic Petroleum business rights to Rising Sun Petroleum and quotes Soviet trade representative L. Kagan’s intention to continue selling oil.

subfiles.title: Teagle’s letter of appreciation
subfiles.about: Thanks State Department and embassy officials for assistance to Standard-Vacuum negotiators.
subfiles.summary: Teagle credits Grew, Neville, Dickover, Hornbeck and Mackay with helping the company’s negotiations in Japan and Manchukuo.

subfiles.title: Division summary of Tokyo despatch No. 1378
subfiles.about: Summarizes prospective oil storage relief and the newly organized Chosen Oil Company.
subfiles.summary: The division expects possible modification of Japan’s six-month storage requirement. It also summarizes assurances that the new Chosen Oil Company would leave foreign firms’ Korean business intact, while noting fears that monopoly policies could spread.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1378: American Oil Interests in Japan
subfiles.about: Discusses the cost of six months’ oil storage and the Chosen Oil Company’s formation.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports Japanese industry’s difficulty funding storage and predicts a possible indefinite delay of the six-month requirement. He describes the new Korean refinery company and conflicting accounts of whether it would preserve foreign companies’ business or introduce an oil monopoly.

subfiles.title: Instruction to Tokyo on oil regulations
subfiles.about: Suggests raising Standard-Vacuum’s concern during a final talk with Japan’s Foreign Minister.
subfiles.summary: The Department leaves it to the ambassador to mention whether Japan will honor its oral assurances.

subfiles.title: Tokyo telegram No. 152 on petroleum regulations
subfiles.about: Reports cabinet consideration and ministerial opposition to modifying Japan’s oil law.
subfiles.summary: Grew says Hirota gave no forecast; Kurusu hoped to settle the matter before October using Japan’s dependence on foreign oil.

subfiles.title: Division note on Tokyo despatch No. 1385
subfiles.about: Highlights disagreement over reducing oil storage to three months.
subfiles.summary: The note flags a possible four-month compromise acceptable to foreign oil firms.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1385: American Oil Interests in Japan
subfiles.about: Reports competing Japanese proposals to alter oil stockholding rules.
subfiles.summary: Yoshino’s proposed three-month limit and a plan assigning longer storage to subsidized Japanese firms met opposition. He was reportedly considering four months for all firms without subsidy.

subfiles.title: Division summary of Tokyo despatch No. 1408
subfiles.about: Summarizes embassy conversations on oil storage and price problems.
subfiles.summary: The division notes military demands for reserves, concern for the Commerce Minister’s reputation and Kurusu’s hope for settlement before October.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1408: American Oil Interests in Japan
subfiles.about: Reports Grew’s talks with Hirota and Kurusu and Japanese debate over oil policy.
subfiles.summary: Neville describes conflicting ministry views on storage, subsidies and gasoline prices. Japanese refiners also sought decisions before committing funds. He encloses two conversation memoranda and a newspaper article criticizing the Petroleum Industry Law.

subfiles.title: Conversation with Hirota
subfiles.about: Records Hirota’s response to an informal inquiry about an oil settlement.
subfiles.summary: Hirota said several ministers would confer and hoped for a favorable result, without predicting one.

subfiles.title: Conversation with Kurusu
subfiles.about: Records Kurusu’s account of ministries’ conflicting oil policy priorities.
subfiles.summary: Kurusu describes military storage demands, resistance to subsidies and political difficulty raising gasoline prices. He says settlement is needed before October.

subfiles.title: Petroleum Act Found in Impasse One Year After Its Enforcement
subfiles.from: P. D. Q., The Osaka Mainichi
subfiles.about: Critiques the Petroleum Act’s storage, price-control and domestic-industry provisions.
subfiles.summary: The article argues that financial burdens and market conditions have frustrated the law’s aims.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1421: American Oil Interests in Japan
subfiles.about: Reports cabinet discussions of storage relief, compensation and gasoline prices.
subfiles.summary: Press accounts suggest officials are considering how to relieve oil firms’ storage burden. Neville considers a plan requiring three months’ stocks from foreign firms and six months from subsidized Japanese firms possible, but no settlement is confirmed.

subfiles.title: File note: American Oil Interests in Japan
subfiles.about: Cross-references despatch No. 1427 on American oil interests.
subfiles.summary: Indexes Neville’s August 9 despatch.

subfiles.title: Relations with the United States: American Oil Interests in Japan
subfiles.about: Summarizes slow progress on oil storage and price questions.
subfiles.summary: The excerpt identifies military demands and the Commerce Minister’s reputation as obstacles and recounts Grew’s inconclusive July talk with Hirota.

subfiles.title: Division summary of Tokyo despatch No. 1443
subfiles.about: Summarizes Machida’s difficulties changing the oil law and Kurusu’s assurance about the October deadline.
subfiles.summary: The division reads Kurusu’s promise of no lawbreakers on October 1 as implying an imminent legal change.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1443: American Oil Interests in Japan
subfiles.about: Reports failed interministerial talks and Kurusu’s assurance that foreign firms would not violate the law on October 1.
subfiles.summary: Newspapers describe rejected plans for storage relief and warn that foreign firms might withdraw if penalized. Kurusu explains Machida’s political difficulties and promises that there will be no lawbreakers on October 1, apparently anticipating a regulatory change.

subfiles.title: Division summary of Tokyo despatch No. 1465
subfiles.about: Summarizes unconfirmed press reports of delayed enforcement and compensation.
subfiles.summary: The note says postponement might avert violations but leave foreign firms uncertain.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1465: American Oil Interests in Japan
subfiles.about: Reviews reported solutions to Japan’s oil storage impasse and the Navy’s search for oil supplies.
subfiles.summary: Press reports point toward postponing six-month storage enforcement, with possible compensation and a modest gasoline price increase; the embassy cannot confirm a decision. Neville explains why delay would leave both foreign firms and the military dissatisfied, summarizes newspaper criticism, and reports Navy interest in domestic drilling, overseas concessions and petroleum substitutes.

subfiles.title: Division memorandum on Tokyo telegram No. 187
subfiles.about: Assesses a possible treaty objection to compulsory oil storage for Japanese national defense.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum says Japan has abandoned the April three-month understanding while postponing six-month enforcement to June 1936. It considers whether uncompensated storage for national defense could be a prohibited military exaction under the 1911 U.S.–Japan treaty. It recommends preparing representations only if compensation proves inadequate, American firms suffer penalties and they request further help.

subfiles.title: Tokyo telegram No. 187
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, U.S. Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports Japan’s decision to postpone, but retain, the six-month storage requirement.
subfiles.summary: Japanese officials say the deadline will move to June 30, 1936, while compensation remains uncertain and firms storing more oil may receive better quotas. Foreign representatives object that this breaks the April understanding. Neville asks whether the national-defense purpose supports an objection under the 1911 treaty.

subfiles.title: Department telegram on possible military exaction
subfiles.about: Sets conditions for considering a treaty protest over uncompensated oil storage.
subfiles.summary: The Department sees a possible military-exaction claim if Standard-Vacuum is inadequately compensated and penalized, and asks the embassy for evidence. It directs the embassy to await instructions before making representations.

subfiles.title: Division summary of Tokyo despatch No. 1482
subfiles.about: Summarizes foreign firms’ objections to Japan’s temporary storage solution.
subfiles.summary: The note records inadequate proposed compensation, concerns about preferential quotas and impending protests over Korean oil quotas.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1482: American Oil Interests in Japan, opening pages
subfiles.about: Reports the Imperial Ordinance postponing six-month oil storage enforcement and foreign companies’ objections.
subfiles.summary: Imperial Ordinance No. 272 permits special storage rules until June 30, 1936, avoiding immediate violations by foreign firms. The firms consider this temporary relief inadequate because six-month storage remains the government’s goal, proposed compensation excludes major costs, and companies that comply early may receive preferential quotas. The despatch continues beyond page 308.
